An OR implementation that treats any nonzero number as true would yield 1 for 2 || -1; the required positive-only truth test yields 0 for that row.
An AND implementation using nonzero rather than positive truthiness would produce 1 for 2 && -1 instead of 0.
An equality implementation returning a difference or boolean text instead of numeric 1/0 would produce different derived cells.
A relational implementation returning boolean text or reversing the comparison would emit a different result for 2 > -1.
A parser that applies addition/subtraction in the wrong associativity or precedence would produce a result other than 4.
A parser that assigns the wrong precedence or associativity to multiplication, division, and modulo would produce a result other than 3.
A parser that treats unary minus as a binary operator or applies it after multiplication would fail or produce a value other than -2.
An evaluator that mishandles function calls, parentheses, column references, or numeric literals would fail or produce a value other than 3.
A program that errors or returns infinity instead of NaN would write a different result for division by zero.
A program that errors or returns a numeric remainder instead of NaN would write a different result for modulo by zero.
A program that treats NaN as equal to zero, or otherwise returns true for this comparison, would produce 1 rather than 0.
A square-root implementation that returns an error or a numeric value for negative input would differ from NaN.
A truncation-based implementation would produce 2 instead of the ceiling value 3.
A ceiling- or truncation-based implementation would produce a value other than 2 for this positive non-integer.
Banker's rounding would produce -2 rather than rounding the half away from zero to -3.
A program that ignores the exponent or reverses the arguments would produce a value other than 8.
A base-10 logarithm implementation would produce a value other than the natural logarithm of 2.
An implementation that returns the larger argument would produce 3 instead of 2.
An implementation that returns the smaller argument would produce 2 instead of 3.
An implementation that chooses the first branch for a false condition would produce 10 instead of 20.
An implementation that fails to clamp values below the lower bound would produce -4 instead of -2.
An implementation that does not substitute the fallback for NaN would output NaN instead of 7.
An evaluator that cannot nest functions would fail or produce a result other than 2.
An implementation that mishandles logical conjunction or relational comparisons would fail to produce 0 for 5 and 20 for 20.
